reasons: The source supports using a roughly six-month period and says 90 days is another possible period, but it does not say to use 90 days specifically when less history exists. It only says historical availability may vary by when Clarity was set up.
The approximately six-month completion criterion is supported.
The substantive principle is supported: the speaker says the Insights block is the important part to focus on, while many listed KPIs are available in Google Analytics.
The asserted depends_on relation to date-range filtering is not established by the excerpt; the speaker presents filtering as a first practice, not as a prerequisite for prioritizing Insights.
The excerpt supports clicking the camera icon to open recordings and watching rage-click recordings when they may warrant a change.
The action overgeneralizes the demonstrated camera-icon behavior from rage clicks to any insight metric. This passage explicitly describes the icon and affected recordings for rage clicks only.
Its depends_on relation to the prior dashboard-prioritization principle is not stated.
The quoted heuristic that rates under 1 to 2 percent are good is supported and is correctly characterized as the speaker's own view.
The unknowns incorrectly describe the observed 0.2% rate as unreconciled with the under-1-to-2% heuristic. A 0.2% rate is compatible with that heuristic.
The source says the speaker would consider watching recordings for all listed insights and says fundamental usability issues should be resolved regardless of percentage.

The candidate turns a conditional recommendation into an unconditional instruction to watch all recordings. The source's qualification is that an actual fundamental usability issue should be resolved, not that every low-rate insight necessarily requires review.
The depends_on relation inherits the prior candidate's unsupported broad claim that the camera-icon workflow applies to all insight types.
The definition accurately reflects the excerpt: a dead click occurs when a user attempts to click an element that is not clickable.
No unsupported threshold, remedy, or platform behavior is added.
The source explicitly presents non-clickable featured-in logos as a scenario in which dead clicks may be acceptable because outbound navigation can conflict with conversion goals.
The candidate preserves the source's qualified framing rather than treating this as a universal rule.
The source explicitly contrasts acceptable dead clicks with elements that should be clickable because they assist the user's conversion journey.
The alternative relation to the prior, conversion-preserving scenario is consistent with the source's stated contrast.
The SaaS pricing example, including that only the free-credits button was clickable while users clicked surrounding pricing elements, is directly supported.
The candidate appropriately does not claim that a particular fix was implemented or that conversion results followed.
The excerpt supports that users clicked a non-clickable centered logo, including rage/dead-click behavior observed in dashboard data and recordings.
The candidate does not add an unsupported claim that the logo was subsequently fixed or that the fix had a measured effect.
The candidate retains the source's conditional interpretation: excessive scrolling can indicate that users cannot find information.
Its trigger correctly reflects the source's description of rapid top-to-bottom scrolling on a page.
The title and claimed warning infer that the speaker advises avoiding time on these metrics, but the quoted source clause is garbled: "so I would really spend too much time there."
The candidate itself acknowledges that a negation may be missing and that the polarity is unresolved. Therefore the excerpt cannot support the asserted avoidance recommendation.
The excerpt directly describes clicking the Heatmaps tab, being shown popular pages, and selecting the homepage in the demonstration.
The candidate accurately retains the distinction between the demo account's two pages and the speaker's statement that accounts typically show five to ten popular pages.
The candidate accurately identifies that the source ends mid-sentence while discussing heat-map screenshots and pop-ups.
It does not infer the missing pop-up effect, platform behavior, or remedy.

source_limitations: The supplied excerpt ends mid-sentence during the heat-map discussion, so the effect of pop-ups on screenshots and any recommended handling cannot be determined from this excerpt.
A purported recommendation about spending time on Google-Analytics-overlapping metrics contains a garbled clause with unresolved polarity: "so I would really spend too much time there."
The excerpt promises fuller recordings and heat-map walkthroughs later, but those procedures are not included here.

The excerpt provides illustrative observations and the speaker's heuristics, but does not provide a defined denominator for insight rates, a universal benchmark, or outcome data for the example fixes.
